title: Scientists Confirm a Third Type of Magnetism
summary: For nearly 90 years, scientists sorted magnetic materials into two groups. Now they have strong proof of a third. A research team led by the U.S. Department of Energy's SLAC National Accelerator Laboratory has found convincing experimental evidence for altermagnetism, a form of magnetism that mixes traits from both older groups. The study was published in the journal Science. The team studied manganese telluride, a material known as MnTe, which had long been classified as an antiferromagnet. In it, they found direct evidence of chirality, a twist in the material's magnetic structure. It is a twist like that of a spiral staircase. That twist is a key sign of altermagnetism. Lead author Daniel Jost of SLAC said the results provide strong confirmation that this third phase is real. Magnetism comes from a property of electrons called spin, often described as up or down. In ferromagnets, the spins line up in the same direction, and together they create the magnetic field of an ordinary magnet. Antiferromagnets, identified in 1933, work differently. Neighboring spins point in opposite directions, so their effects cancel out and no overall magnetism appears. Altermagnets are different again. Their spins alternate, like antiferromagnets, so they show no overall magnetization. Yet they can also carry useful spin currents, a trick linked to ferromagnets. In altermagnets, the crystal patterns around oppositely pointing spins are rotated compared with each other, breaking a symmetry found in ordinary antiferromagnets. That small difference changes how electrons behave. The term altermagnets dates to 2022, and the new study supplies the missing proof. The discovery could also lead to practical uses, including advanced memory systems, quantum devices, and more energy-efficient data centers.
why_it_matters: Altermagnets could make the memory chips and data centers behind everyday devices faster and use less energy, so this discovery may shape the technology that powers the computers and gadgets children use every day.
